meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.trans: Are you running away again today?
And we are only dating starting today.
Today will be our first day.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('we') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Hey there, who do we have here?
We have been friends for a very long time.
And we are only dating starting today.

избавиться.gloss: to get rid of, to be rid of

meanings.en: to get rid of, to be rid of
meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (root 'бавиться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to get rid of', forming an aspectual pair with 'избавляться'.

examples.text: Сегодня мы избавимся от Германа навсегда.
examples.trans: Today we will get rid of German forever.

examples.text: Ты хотел избавиться от моей жены?
examples.trans: Did you want to get rid of my wife.

examples.text: Нам нужно срочно избавиться от этого старого дивана.
examples.trans: We urgently need to get rid of this old sofa.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'from' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.text: Говори, у меня от коллег нет секретов.
examples.trans: Speak, I have no secrets from colleagues.

examples.text: Феде сейчас так хорошо от таблеток.
examples.trans: Fedya feels so good from the pills right now.

examples.text: Сегодня мы избавимся от Германа навсегда.
examples.trans: Today we will get rid of German forever.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'forever', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Tell me about this German.
I am talking about your German.

examples.text: Этот повар увёл у Германа жену.
examples.trans: That cook stole German's wife from him.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'forever'.

examples.text: Сегодня мы избавимся от Германа навсегда.
examples.trans: Today we will get rid of German forever.
Leave this place forever!
They parted forever.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: Chef, come on, do not keep us in suspense.

examples.text: Шеф, у меня есть отличная идея.
examples.trans: Chef, I have a great idea.

examples.text: Шеф, мы там чуть не попались.
examples.trans: Chef, we almost got caught in there.

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (root 'сказать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to tell', forming an aspectual pair with 'рассказывать'.

examples.trans: Tell me about this German.
Come along, I will tell you everything.

examples.text: Шеф, расскажите, пожалуйста, весь ваш план.
examples.trans: Chef, please tell us your whole plan.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('please') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Шеф, расскажите, пожалуйста, весь ваш план.
examples.trans: Chef, please tell us your whole plan.

examples.text: В чём дело? Будьте аккуратнее, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What is the matter? Be more careful, please.
A coffee, please.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.
Good morning to all of you.
Thank you, everything is very tasty.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: А вот это разве не ваш нож?
examples.trans: Isn't this one right here your knife?

examples.text: Шеф, расскажите, пожалуйста, весь ваш план.
examples.trans: Chef, please tell us your whole plan.

examples.text: Не хотела, чтобы ваш вечер испортился.
examples.trans: I did not want your evening to be ruined.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'plan', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Но у меня планы на вечер.
examples.trans: But I have plans for the evening.

examples.text: Шеф, расскажите, пожалуйста, весь ваш план.
examples.trans: Chef, please tell us your whole plan.
The mayor came up with a new plan.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'at first'.

examples.trans: First they were rude and insulting over there.
Let's start everything from the beginning.

examples.text: Мы танцевали. Сначала они там грубили, оскорбляли.
examples.trans: We were dancing. First they were rude and insulting over there.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'deprive', forming an aspectual pair with 'лишать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Сначала мы лишим его этих таблеток.
examples.trans: First we will deprive him of those pills.
They suspended his driver's license.

examples.text: Ого! А меня вчера лишили прав!
examples.trans: Whoa! And they suspended my license yesterday!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('he') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Stop it, I know him well.
He used to work in Riga.
Give me the phone, I will call him.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('this') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: You need to defeat this shark.
Why did you make this shark?

examples.text: Этот повар увёл у Германа жену.
examples.trans: That cook stole German's wife from him.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'pill', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Kostya, what, are you on pills?

examples.text: Слушайте, а Герман всё время пьёт таблетки.
examples.trans: Listen, German is taking pills all the time.
Really? What pills is he taking?

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (root 'манить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to lure', forming an aspectual pair with 'заманивать'.

examples.trans: We will lure him into a trap.

examples.text: Надо заманить его на свою территорию.
examples.trans: You need to lure him onto your territory.

examples.text: Надо заманить его на свою территорию. Там, где ты сильный.
examples.trans: You need to lure him onto your territory. Right where you are strong.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: He used to work in Riga.
It happened in Riga.
And in the end she agreed.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'trap', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: We will lure him into a trap.

examples.text: Сегодня мы избавимся от Германа навсегда.
examples.trans: Today we will get rid of German forever.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And in the end she agreed.
He is a psychopath and very aggressive.

examples.text: И все деньги у него украли.
examples.trans: And they stole all his money from him.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to interrupt', forming an aspectual pair with 'прерывать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: И прервём на самом интересном месте.
examples.trans: And we will interrupt at the most interesting part.
You interrupted such a dream of mine!
Excuse me for interrupting you.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, можно тебя на минуту?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, may I have a minute with you?
Dima, let's step aside for a minute.

examples.text: Иди лучше спокойно работай на кухне.
examples.trans: Better go work quietly in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'the most', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: The most important thing is the people.
It's the biggest town.
Do you know the main thing?

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'interesting', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: И прервём на самом интересном месте.
examples.trans: And we will interrupt at the most interesting part.
This is a very interesting book.
Funny you should say that!

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'place', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: You lost your place yourself.

examples.text: И прервём на самом интересном месте.
examples.trans: And we will interrupt at the most interesting part.
This is my seat.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: But just one spark is enough.
But suddenly a cook walked in there.

examples.text: Но достать её придётся тебе самой.
examples.trans: But you will have to get it out yourself.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'necessary'.

examples.trans: I need to make a call.
You need to rest.

examples.text: Мне нужно позвонить губернатору. Дай телефон.
examples.trans: I need to call the governor. Give me a phone.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.

examples.trans: I feel very good with you.
Stop it, I know him well.

examples.text: Феде сейчас так хорошо от таблеток.
examples.trans: Fedya feels so good from the pills right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (root 'огреть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to warm up', forming an aspectual pair with 'разогревать'.

examples.text: Но сначала его нужно хорошо разогреть.
examples.trans: But first we need to warm him up well.
The chocolate needs to be melted.
How much chocolate needs to be melted?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('maybe') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Maybe tomorrow.
I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'together'.

examples.trans: All right, let's go have breakfast together.

examples.text: Вика, может, мы сегодня вместе поужинаем?
examples.trans: Vika, maybe we could have dinner together tonight?
We're together.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'ужинать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have dinner', forming an aspectual pair with 'ужинать'.

examples.text: Вика, может, мы сегодня вместе поужинаем?
examples.trans: Vika, maybe we could have dinner together tonight?

examples.text: Мы поужинаем сегодня у меня дома.
examples.trans: We will have dinner tonight at my place.
Where can we have dinner?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
No, I am not running away.
Do you feel bad with me right now?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.trans: Do you feel bad with me right now?
We have a lot of work right now.
I will slice everything up quickly right now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (root 'казать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to order', forming an aspectual pair with 'заказывать'.

examples.trans: They ordered a horsemeat steak out there.

examples.text: Я сейчас закажу нам хороший столик.
examples.trans: I will book a nice table for us right now.

examples.text: Спасибо, но я уже всё заказала.
examples.trans: Thank you, but I have already ordered everything.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'good', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Я сейчас закажу нам хороший столик.
examples.trans: I will book a nice table for us right now.
A good day.
What a lovely morning!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'small table', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Я сейчас закажу нам хороший столик.
examples.trans: I will book a nice table for us right now.

examples.text: Они заняли свободный столик у окна.
examples.trans: They took a free table near the window.
Would you like to sit at an available table?

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian interj meaning 'thank you', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you, everything is very tasty.
Thank you very much for the information.

examples.text: Ладно, спасибо, ты мне поднял настроение.
examples.trans: All right, thanks, you lifted my spirits.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'already'.

examples.trans: Have you two been dating for a long time?
We have been friends for a very long time.
And we already saw what happened next.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: Hey there, who do we have here?
It has the exact same title.

examples.text: Катюша, у меня всё уже готово.
examples.trans: Katyusha, I have everything ready already.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'at home'.

examples.trans: The main thing is, you keep him at home.
Today I'm staying at home.

examples.text: А Осипенко сейчас дома лежит. У него больное сердце.
examples.trans: And Osipenko is lying at home right now. He has a sick heart.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('here') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А вот это разве не ваш нож?
examples.trans: Isn't this one right here your knife?
That is the kind of handsome man he is.
Here is Viktoriya Sergeyevna's favorite wine.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'favourite', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Сейчас, любимая, уже несу твой чай!
examples.trans: Right away, sweetheart, I am bringing your tea already!
Here is Viktoriya Sergeyevna's favorite wine.

examples.text: А ты готовишь мой любимый торт со сгущёнкой!
examples.trans: And you make my favourite condensed milk cake!

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'wine', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Here is Viktoriya Sergeyevna's favorite wine.
This is very good wine.
A glass of red wine.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'Victoria', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'Sergeyevna', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'may'.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, можно тебя на минуту?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, may I have a minute with you?

examples.text: А можно мне ещё одну таблетку?
examples.trans: May I have one more pill?
May I take this bottle?

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to take', forming an aspectual pair with 'брать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: May I take this bottle?
Go and hire Galileo.
Take the money.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'bottle', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: May I take this bottle?
With a bottle of wine in your hand?
Buy a bottle of water.
